title: Mara and the Language
premise: Ines Iversen, a translator in Oslo who has spent thirty years quietly losing her mother's coastal dialect, keeps a notebook of the words she can no longer remember and the things she never said to her family. When a radio broadcast airs a folk song she knows was written by her grandmother and never recorded, Ines realizes someone from her childhood village is still alive—and still keeping the language she abandoned. Returning north to confront the estranged aunt who raised her and the boy she loved and left, Ines must choose between the safe invisibility of translation and speaking, finally, in her own voice. The story ends with Ines recording her aunt's songs as the old woman dies, accepting that a language survives not by being preserved but by being passed on.
about_author: Ansel Halloran is the pen name of a former interpreter who spent a decade working between Nordic languages before turning to fiction. They write about inheritance, silence, and the small betrayals that hold families together.

chapters.title: The Inventory
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. A meticulous translator in Oslo, Ines maintains a notebook of dying words and unsaid sentences, including one addressed to her estranged aunt Marta. Her ordered life cracks when a late-night radio program plays a song she knows was composed privately by her grandmother decades ago—never written down, never recorded. The emotional beat: dread disguised as curiosity, as the past announces it has been waiting for her.

chapters.title: What the Radio Knew
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, with flashbacks to age sixteen. She traces the broadcast to a folklorist who recorded songs in her home village last summer, and learns Marta sang for him. Flashbacks reveal young Ines's love for Eirik, the fisherman's son, and the night she chose a scholarship over both him and the dialect. Emotional beat: guilt sharpening into resolve; she buys a train ticket north.

chapters.title: The House That Kept Its Voice
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. In the village, Marta receives her coldly but cannot hide her failing memory—or the notebook of songs she has guarded for fifty years. Eirik, now widowed, forces Ines to admit why she really left: not duty, but fear of being known. When Marta mistakes Ines for her dead sister and sings the radio song directly to her, Ines breaks. Climax: grief, accusation, and the first honest sentence she has spoken in years.

chapters.title: Borrowed Words
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, closing with Marta's. With weeks left, Ines stays, recording Marta's songs and teaching herself the words in her inventory until the notebook empties. She and Eirik make no promises, only a beginning. On the last morning, Marta asks Ines to sing one back to her—and she does, imperfectly, in their shared tongue. Resolution: identity reclaimed not as recovery but as choice.
